article.title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?
article.subtitle: *Statistically* biased, we mean. A guide to house effects in the Silver Bulletin model.

extraction.summary: Explains how the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model and polling averages apply house effects adjustments to polls, separate from poll weighting. House effects are estimated by comparing each firm's polls to the trendline of other polls, iterating between trendline and house-effect estimation. The more highly rated nonpartisan firms anchor the process. Estimates are mean-reverted: firms with few polls are shrunk toward zero if nonpartisan, and toward a partisan-bias prior of about 3 points if they have a partisan sponsor. The article also gives current house effects by pollster, separate Harris and Trump vote-share house effects, and notes on weighting (aggressive recency, sample size, and spreading weight across a prolific firm's polls).

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin polling averages are 'aggressive': they put a big premium on newer data, i.e. heavy recency weighting. Other good models use less aggressive recency weighting.
findings.rationale: Acknowledged as a legitimate design choice that others make differently.
findings.evidence_quote: our polling averages are pretty aggressive — meaning we put a big premium on newer data. Other excellent models take a less aggressive approach.

findings.statement: In the Silver Bulletin model, sample size is a major factor in a poll's influence (weight) score.
findings.evidence_quote: The sample size is also a big factor in a given poll's influence score.

findings.statement: When a firm frequently polls the same race (national or the same state), as YouGov and Morning Consult do, the Silver Bulletin model spreads a total firm-level weight across that firm's surveys rather than giving each poll full weight.
findings.rationale: Otherwise the averages would quickly be dominated by the more prolific pollsters.
findings.evidence_quote: the model essentially spreads the total weight assigned to a polling firm across those different surveys; otherwise our averages would quickly be dominated by the more prolific pollsters

findings.statement: A poll's weight in the Silver Bulletin model combines pollster rating, recency, sample size and the firm-level weight-spreading for prolific firms. The pollster ratings alone show quality absent those other factors.
findings.evidence_quote: To see our assessment of pollster quality absent those other factors, just bookmark our pollster ratings.

findings.statement: Different polling averages' weighting schemes mostly end up in highly similar places, with RealClearPolitics as the exception.
findings.rationale: Complaining about weighting schemes is generally not a good use of time.
findings.evidence_quote: other than RealClearPolitics, they mostly wind up in highly similar places

findings.statement: Besides weighting, the Silver Bulletin model applies a house effects adjustment to each poll, correcting for a firm's consistent lean toward Democrats or Republicans. A heavily weighted poll may still be adjusted heavily.
findings.rationale: Makes the polling averages more stable and strips out firms' statistical bias toward certain candidates.
findings.evidence_quote: even if a poll that's known to lean toward Donald Trump or Kamala Harris gets a large weight in our forecast, it's often being adjusted heavily on the backend

findings.statement: House effects measure statistical bias, not political bias. The two sometimes correlate and sometimes don't; Fox News's polling department is unbiased despite its editorial slant.
findings.evidence_quote: By "bias", we mean statistical bias. Sometimes this correlates with political bias and sometimes this doesn't

findings.statement: House effects for the 2024 Harris race use only Harris/Trump polls. No leftover Biden/Trump matchup data is used after the candidate switch.
findings.evidence_quote: We don't use any leftover data from the Biden/Trump matchup.

findings.statement: Published house effects are mean-reverted estimates, meant to approximate a pollster's long-run house effect if it surveyed the race every day. Firms with only a handful of polls are shrunk heavily toward the mean; prolific firms such as Morning Consult get more precise, less-shrunk estimates.
findings.evidence_quote: If a pollster has only conducted a handful of polls, its house effects are discounted heavily toward the mean

findings.statement: For nonpartisan polls, house effects are mean-reverted toward a prior of zero.

quantities.name: prior mean for nonpartisan house effect

findings.evidence_quote: For nonpartisan polls, house effects are reverted toward a mean of zero.

findings.statement: Polls with partisan sponsors are treated as 'biased until proven unbiased'. Their house effect prior is a lean toward the sponsor's candidate, because presidential partisan-sponsored polls typically exaggerate their candidate's margin by about 3 points, and the model accounts for this.
findings.evidence_quote: Presidential polls with partisan sponsors typically exaggerate their candidate's margin by about 3 percentage points and the model accounts for this.

findings.statement: Partisan classification depends on the poll's sponsor, not the polling firm, since some firms poll for both partisan and nonpartisan sponsors. The exception is Trafalgar Group, which is always treated as inherently Republican.
findings.rationale: Trafalgar has a history of failing to disclose who it conducts polls for.
findings.evidence_quote: it's the sponsor of a poll that matters in this calculation, not the polling firm

findings.statement: House effects are calculated by comparing a firm's polls to the trendline of other polls of the same state, or to other national polls for national surveys.
findings.evidence_quote: we basically look at how a firm's polls compare to the trendline of other polls from that state (or compared to other national polls)

findings.statement: House effect estimation is iterative. The model computes trendlines, estimates house effects against them, recomputes trendlines with house-effect-adjusted polls, re-estimates house effects, and so on.
findings.evidence_quote: we calculate the trendlines, then calculate the house effects based on the trendlines, then recalculate the trendlines with adjustments for house effects

findings.statement: In the iterative house-effect process, the more highly rated nonpartisan firms act as the center of gravity: the 'true' values against which other firms are compared. As a result, top-rated firms tend to show little net house effect.
findings.evidence_quote: the more highly rated, nonpartisan firms serve as essentially the center of gravity: the "true" values against which other firms are compared

findings.statement: A raw poll result is shifted by the firm's house effect. An R+1 Rasmussen poll (house effect −2.6 on Harris margin) is treated roughly like a D+2 poll, while an R+1 NYT/Siena poll is treated essentially as R+1.
findings.evidence_quote: If we get an R +1 Rasmussen poll for example, the model thinks about it more like a D +2 poll due to Rasmussen's large house effect.

findings.statement: The model calculates separate house effects for each candidate's vote share (Harris and Trump), not just the margin, because pollsters differ in how many undecided or third-party voters they show. The net margin house effect is roughly Harris house effect minus Trump house effect.
findings.rationale: Some pollsters show more undecided voters than others.
findings.evidence_quote: we technically calculate separate house effects for Harris's and Trump's vote shares because some pollsters show more undecided voters than others

findings.statement: YouGov has negative house effects for both Harris (−0.6) and Trump (−0.5), meaning more undecided or third-party voters but little net house effect. Marist has positive house effects for both candidates (table: Harris +0.5, Trump +0.2).
findings.evidence_quote: YouGov actually has negative house effects for both Harris (-0.6) and Trump (-0.5)

findings.statement: Mean-reverted house effects on Harris margin as of Sept 27, 2024, for pollsters with at least 5 Harris/Trump polls. Democratic-leaning: Ipsos +1.9, Outward Intelligence +1.9, PPP +1.4, Morning Consult +1.2, Big Village +1.0, Bullfinch +0.8, Change Research +0.7, UNH +0.4, Focaldata +0.4, Benenson/GS +0.3, Marist +0.3, SurveyUSA +0.3, MassINC +0.2, Fox (Beacon/Shaw) +0.1, TIPP +0.1, Suffolk +0.0. Near zero or slightly Republican-leaning: Quinnipiac −0.0, YouGov −0.0, NYT/Siena −0.1, Fabrizio/Impact −0.1, SSRS (CNN) −0.1, POS −0.1, Emerson −0.3, FAU/Mainstreet −0.3, Patriot Polling −0.3. Republican-leaning: GSG/GBAO (Navigator) −0.4, RMG −0.4, Redfield & Wilton −0.5, Cygnal −0.8, InsiderAdvantage −0.8, Harris Insights & Analytics −1.3, Capitol Weekly −1.5, Spry −2.3, Rasmussen −2.6, Trafalgar −2.7.

Separate vote-share house effects (Harris, Trump) with poll counts and pollster ratings, from the table as of Sept 27, 2024: NYT/Siena 16 polls, A+, −0.3/−0.2; Fox (Beacon/Shaw) 13, A, −0.1/−0.2; Cygnal 7, A, −0.6/+0.1; Marist 10, A, +0.5/+0.2; SurveyUSA 15, A, −0.1/−0.3; Emerson 37, A-, +0.3/+0.6; POS 5, A-, −0.1/+0.0; PPP 15, A-, +0.1/−1.3; Quinnipiac 9, A-, +0.0/+0.0; Suffolk 5, A-, −0.4/−0.4; MassINC 5, A/B, +0.2/−0.0; TIPP 9, A/B, −0.6/−0.7; Harris Insights & Analytics 10, B+, +0.2/+1.5; Trafalgar 11, B+, −1.6/+1.0; YouGov 40, B+, −0.6/−0.5; Big Village 8, B, −0.9/−1.9; InsiderAdvantage 15, B, −0.5/+0.3; Rasmussen 21, B, −1.3/+1.3; Change Research 6, B-, −0.3/−1.1; Ipsos 14, B-, −0.6/−2.5.

quantities.name: minimum polls for inclusion in chart

findings.statement: Pollster rating and house effect are distinct. Firms with large partisan house effects can still be rated reasonably well, e.g. Trafalgar (B+) and Rasmussen (B). Most of the highest-rated firms have little net house effect.
findings.evidence_quote: most of our most highly-rated firms have little net house effect

findings.statement: In some elections, highly rated polls and mediocre polls diverge systematically; for example, higher-quality polls were usually more favorable to Obama in 2012. In such cases, anchoring house effects to top-rated firms matters. In 2024 this divergence was not present, so an average built only from top firms would look about the same as the Silver Bulletin average.
findings.evidence_quote: Higher-quality polls were usually more favorable to Barack Obama in 2012 than lower-rated ones, for instance. But 2024 isn't one of those elections.

findings.statement: Silver criticizes 'unskewing' polls by scrutinizing odd crosstabs, such as recalled 2020 vote in narrow subgroups. He says a bad poll for one's candidate can simply reflect sampling variation.
findings.evidence_quote: Could a bad poll for your favorite candidate just come down to sampling variation?

findings.statement: Seeming outlier polls are kept rather than discarded, because they can give critical clues about how the race is trending. Only consistent leans are adjusted, via house effects.
findings.evidence_quote: Even seeming "outlier" polls can provide critical clues as to how the race is trending. But if a pollster consistently leans toward Trump or Harris, we adjust

political_insights.insight: In late September 2024, top-rated pollsters disagreed among themselves rather than diverging as a group from lower-rated ones. NYT/Siena had some bad data for Harris, while Selzer showed Harris down only 4 in Iowa.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Quality-only averages would not change the picture much in 2024.

open_questions: Exact shrinkage formula for mean-reverting house effects (prior strength, dependence on number of polls).
How the roughly 3-point partisan-sponsor prior is applied: as the prior mean, and how fast it updates with data.
Number of iterations or convergence criterion in the trendline/house-effect iterative procedure.
How much weight each highly rated firm gets in anchoring the center of gravity.
Recency decay function and sample-size weighting formula for the polling averages.
Exact formula for spreading firm-level weight across a prolific pollster's surveys.
Whether house effects are pooled across states and national polls or estimated per jurisdiction.
